[BLR] Workshops - 2.title: Architecture as Code
[BLR] Workshops - 2.description:
Corporations spend millions of dollars and thousands of hours onboarding new people to development teams and troubleshooting incidents where nobody knows who owns what. Tribal knowledge remains locked in individuals' heads while PowerPoint diagrams and Visio files scatter across shared drives like "a novel written on napkins and sticky notes." Traditional tools simply cannot handle modern enterprise complexity.

This workshop introduces Architecture as Code (AaC), a paradigm shift that treats architectural artifacts as version-controlled software assets. According to TOGAF, architecture encompasses the fundamental concepts and relationships of a system. "As Code" means expressing these in text-based, human-readable formats stored alongside the software they describe, with semantic URIs for cross-referencing and the ability to build holistic models from multiple sources.

Participants will learn to implement diagrams using tools like Structurizr DSL and Drawio, enforce policies with Open Policy Agent, and manage Architecture Decision Records programmatically. We will explore dimensions of expansion including metamodels, federated architecture models, progressive elaboration, and integration with AI agents for human-in-the-loop workflows. By the end of this session, participants will be equipped to establish a single source of truth that can be branched, merged, reviewed, and evolved - readable by both humans and machines.

Key Topics

Evolution from manual documentation to codified architecture

TOGAF definition and "As Code" principles

Infrastructure as Code, Diagrams as Code, Policy as Code

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

C4 Model and metamodel extension

Automated validation and compliance checking

Dimensions of expansion: progressive elaboration, integrations, federation

AI agents and human-in-the-loop architectural workflows

Best practices for organizational adoption

 - Branchless change model
 - No working tree / index
 - Easy amending/changing commits
 - Automatic rebases
 - First-class conflicts
 - Undo/redo functionality

In this talk, we'll discuss these concepts and try them out together. We will not need 2 hours, just about an hour (there is no option in the tool for a 1 hour hands-on workshop).

[NCE] Workshops - 3.title: Let's break things with Chaos Engineering

Chaos Engineering is a discipline that helps engineers proactively identify weaknesses and vulnerabilities in their systems by intentionally injecting failures and disruptions (which mean finding issues by breaking things).

This workshop aims to provide you with a better understanding of Chaos Engineering and how it can be implemented in using the tool LitmusChaos.

Let's take on the role of Chaos scientists, creating disruptions through Chaos Experiments to simulate some network failures for example.
Breaking things is fun but let's discover how we can transform these disruptions into tests that validate the strength of systems using the notion of probes.
LitmusChaos also offers convenient features, such as code sharing, that we will explore together.

[NCE] Java Cloud Native track.title: Hey, Quarkus on JVM, can you get any faster? Towards faster builds and faster startup of Quarkus apps on JVM.
[NCE] Java Cloud Native track.description:
Speaker: Guillaume Smet (Red Hat /IBM)

Quarkus is faster than your traditional Java framework, we all know that, right? But can it get faster than itself?

We've spent years obsessing over Quarkus startup time and runtime performance. Build times, on the other hand, didn’t get nearly the same attention. And that was a mistake. Faster builds mean a tighter feedback loop for developers and fewer resources burned in CI.

In this session, we'll start with an overview of the work we've done in recent releases to significantly speed up the build of Quarkus JVM applications.

Now that we got our builds faster, could we also start our JVM applications faster?
As it turns out, yes. We'll present what Project Leyden and AOT class loading can bring to Quarkus (and, more broadly, to Java itself). We’ll cover the improvements we've made, the limitations we're still wrestling with, and why Leyden is reshaping the Java startup performance landscape.

Expect flame graphs, war stories, and technical details you didn't know you cared about. The session stays accessible, though, no deep Quarkus background required.

Room 1.title: Making LLMs Behave Smarter in Development
Room 1.description:
Have you ever wondered why a model, trained on the entire knowledge of internet, sometimes still hallucinates about a library that doesn't exist, keeps forgetting small details as time goes by, or gets your current existing code (or your prompt itself) completely wrong?

We often think of LLMs as some real person standing right in front of us and chatting with us, but underneath, what drives its "next-token prediction" mechanism is actually the application of heavy linear algebra with backpropagation, together with probability theory. Understanding this architecture and realizing its powerful sides (as well as its flaws) is the first step towards making effective use of these tools.

In this 25-minute talk, we will focus on __**context window management**__. 

We are going to explore why "chatting" with LLMs is the wrong paradigm for engineering tasks, why outdated information persists even in top-tier models (and features like web search or RAG cannot fully overcome it), and how can we -at least partially- take manual steps in solving the current problems of LLM usage in development. 

# Content
We are going to go over some simple but verified, researched "tips and tricks" for the purpose of reaching reliability while using LLMs: 
#### "Frontloading"
What I like to describe as "Frontloading" (a technique to exploit attention mechanisms of LLMs by placing critical keywords and sentences with upmost importance at the very beginning and end of your prompts)
#### The "One-shot" approach
Why you should be starting a new chat for every major task and performing manual conversation summarization, rather than letting the agent (or the text editor/IDE itself) dissect and dilute the context of your past conversation history
#### GitIngest
A new, simple, small, but very powerful web-based tool that allows you to dump specific GitHub path URLs (like documentation folders of frameworks, tools, or libraries) into a single Markdown file
#### Custom Context Injection
How to make use of custom Markdown (.md) files together with GitHub Copilot custom instructions in a meaningful way.
#### A brief look at other new cutting-edge tools currently under development
Finally, we'll only have a brief look at the cutting-edge, still-under-development tools like __**specs.md**__ and __**btca**__ to automatize what we discussed earlier. 
##### **specs.md**
Thanks to specs.md,  instead of asking an AI to "build a login page", you can first collaborate with the AI to write a detailed specification in a Markdown file. Once the spec is finalized, you "freeze" it, and the AI agent uses it as its main guide for generating code. It is aimed at preventing hallucinations by forcing the model to follow a documented plan rather than making probabilistic guesses. 
##### **RAG-as-a-Service (?): btca (better context for agents)**
btca (btca.dev) is a tool and protocol currently under development, to solve the "outdated knowledge" problem in LLMs and 'streamline' the process of providing it with up-to-date context. 
You add a btca.config to your project; then, it finds your dependencies by scanning your repository for files related to dependency management (requirements.txt, package.json, pom.xmls etc...) and fetches the latest documentation, for agents to use. It's being designed to automatically inject the most recent API references into your agent's context window.

Room 1.title: From bad architecture to a (maybe) better architecture

## 1. How the PoC Became a Production Problem
I started this project by building a simple Proof of Concept meant only to validate the integration between a traditional operational workflow and an AI component. My intention was always to discard the PoC afterward and build a proper, production‑ready cloud‑native architecture. But inside the organization, that distinction wasn’t fully understood. People began using the PoC as if it were a real system, even loading production data into it. Suddenly I found myself explaining why something that “already worked” couldn’t support real workloads, why it lacked security, resilience, observability, and why keeping it in production was far more expensive and risky than rebuilding it correctly. What seemed like a technical issue quickly turned into a deeper cultural and economic challenge: the team didn’t understand the purpose—or the limitations—of a PoC.

## 2. What I Did to Fix It
To move forward, I focused on educating the team and communicating clearly what was at stake. I walked them through the risks, the missing engineering practices, and the long‑term costs of relying on a prototype. Then I led the migration toward a robust cloud‑native architecture with proper security, CI/CD, observability, data governance, and scalable integration with AI. We ran both systems in parallel, migrated data safely, and gradually decommissioned the PoC without impacting operations. In the end, I not only delivered a stable, secure, and scalable platform, but also helped shift the organization’s understanding of what it means to build technology the right way—showing that overcoming cultural resistance can be just as important as solving the technical problems.

And that is precisely the purpose of this talk: to walk you through both sides of the journey. I want to show the architecture not only from a technical perspective—how it was designed, secured, scaled, and migrated—but also from the cultural perspective, where the biggest challenges often live. My goal is to illustrate how technical excellence and cultural alignment must work together, and how understanding both is essential when transforming a PoC into a real, reliable, cloud‑native solution.

Room 2.title: Inside the Mind of a Machine: Demystifying Large Language Models

Designed for a general audience, this talk connects the technical foundations—tokenization, attention, neural network internals, supervised fine‑tuning, reinforcement learning, and RLHF—to the practical reality of working with AI today. The goal is to replace mystery with intuition, and empower everyone to use these systems more effectively, creatively, and responsibly in their work and life.

Room 2.title: Why Your Azure Disk Isn’t Slow — Your VM Is: Understanding and Fixing Throughput Bottlenecks
Room 2.description:
Cloud workloads can run surprisingly slow even when backed by high‑end Premium or Ultra disks. The real culprit is often overlooked: Azure Virtual Machines have their own IOPS and throughput caps, and these limits can silently throttle disks that are otherwise capable of much higher performance. This mismatch leads to warnings such as “The current VM size supports 23 MBps while attached disks require 160 MBps.”

In this fast, practical, engineering‑focused session, we’ll break down how Azure’s storage pipeline works—uncached I/O paths, cached I/O behavior, baseline vs burst throughput, and the performance limits defined by different VM and disk SKUs. You’ll learn why attaching a higher‑tier disk does not automatically guarantee higher performance, and how to read Azure’s published SKU specifications to identify mismatches before they become production bottlenecks.

The session includes a lightweight, Azure‑Monitor‑free demonstration using standard benchmarking tools such as fio or DiskSpd to validate real disk throughput and clearly illustrate VM‑level bottlenecking. We’ll also walk through a simple, repeatable framework for selecting the right VM size based on workload throughput needs, disk requirements, and expected traffic bursts.

Attendees will leave with the knowledge and tools needed to prevent disk throttling, size their infrastructure more effectively, and ensure their workloads achieve the performance they were designed for—without guesswork, surprises, or expensive over‑provisioning.

Room 3.title: From Cloud to Basement - my personal journey to self hosting everything*
Room 3.description:
TL;DR: A personal, practical look at why I ditched using proprietary software on the cloud and instead rebuilt my digital life using only open source running on hardware at home.
-----
While Amadeus has spent the past years moving from self‑hosted systems in Erding to Microsoft Azure, I’ve been heading in the opposite direction—away from cloud services and proprietary platforms, and toward running (mostly) open‑source software on hardware in my own basement.

Why make that shift? Recent events have shown how fragile our dependence on centralized services can be: the OVH data‑center fire in Strasbourg, major DNS outages at Cloudflare, and even governments blocking access to parts of the internet. Add to that the growing pressure on cloud and software providers to introduce backdoors, and the result is a landscape where user data, privacy, and autonomy feel increasingly at risk. At the same time, subscription costs keep climbing. It’s no surprise that more people are looking for digital sovereignty—control over their data, their infrastructure, and their costs.

In this session, I’ll walk through my own journey back to self‑hosting, using real examples from my setup, including:

- Network and infrastructure
- Hypervisor, storage, and backup
- Remote access
- Self‑hosted applications  
  - Docker, reverse proxying, note taking, flight & country tracking, file storage, photo backup, LLMs for chat and coding, and plenty more
- Future evolution of the setup

My goal is to show that self‑hosting isn’t just for people with racks of hardware and endless free time. You can build something powerful—or something simple—whether you have a dedicated server room or just an old laptop or Raspberry Pi. If this talk nudges you to start your own journey, or simply demystifies what’s possible, then it has done its job.

Disclaimer: This is one person’s setup, shaped by personal needs and preferences. It’s not perfect, and it’s certainly not the only way to do things.

I’ll share how I use templates, the Tasks plugin, and daily/weekly notes to structure my work. Finally, we’ll explore how Obsidian’s Markdown‑based knowledge base integrates naturally with modern AI tools, turning your notes into a powerful private knowledge source you can query from your IDE.

Attendees will leave with a clear understanding of **why** Obsidian stands out, and **what it enables that other tools simply can’t**.

[ERD] Workshops - 2.title: Turning Problem Management into a Driver of Stability and Service Excellence
[ERD] Workshops - 2.description:
Problem Management is often seen as a retrospective exercise—find the root cause, document it, and move on. But what if our reviews became the engine for **real, measurable improvement**?

 

In this talk, we’ll **challenge the traditional approach** to Problem Management Reviews and go **beyond root cause analysis**. We’ll demystify what good improvement actually looks like in practice—and how to make it stick.

Join us to see an **introduction from Stephane Claude** and we explore together how to:

- Translate insights into **high‑impact quality improvements**

- Define and track **meaningful corrective actions** that actually reduce risk

- Assess action items not just by existence, but by **age, criticality, and effectiveness**

- Shift the conversation from “closed” actions to **sustained outcomes**

- Build a culture of **continuous improvement** that strengthens service stability over time

This session is about moving from **analysis to action**, from **reactive fixes to proactive stability**, and from **process compliance to customer impact**. Whether you’re running reviews, contributing to them, or depending on their outcomes, you’ll leave with a clearer understanding of how Problem Management can directly enable **more reliable services and improved customer experiences.**

[ERD] Workshops - 2.title: Stop the Spend Spiral: Intelligent Cost Anomaly Detection Before Budget Impact
[ERD] Workshops - 2.description:
Is your Azure bill a monthly surprise? What if your monitoring system could learn your spending patterns, detect anomalies automatically, and visually show you exactly what changed and why?
 
In this session, I'll show you how to build a production-ready Azure FinOps system that protects enterprise-scale budgets and identifies significant savings opportunities—using only native Azure services. We'll combine Azure Monitor's statistical queries, interactive Workbooks for root cause analysis, and Logic Apps for intelligent notifications.
 
You'll see live:
    - Statistical anomaly detection using Z-score analysis in KQL (adapts to YOUR patterns)
    - Azure Workbooks that automatically correlate cost spikes with configuration changes
    - Visual timelines linking VM resizing, performance metrics, and cost impact
    - Multi-tier budget protection with ML-powered forecasting
    - Complete deployment in <10 minutes via Infrastructure as Code

No more spreadsheet investigations—watch an Azure Workbook automatically identify that a VM SKU change caused a major cost increase, then validate whether it was justified based on performance metrics.

[ERD] Workshops - 2.title: Less Noise, Faster Action: Automating Batch Incidents Handling with Victor
[ERD] Workshops - 2.description:
Operations improvement doesn’t always need a new platform—sometimes it’s one focused initiative that removes a daily drain of human attention. In this talk, I’ll share how we took a high-volume Control‑M incident stream and turned it into an automated, end‑to‑end workflow in Victor: ingest incident updates from MQ, enrich each IR with Control‑M job context (status, job details, output/log signals), and apply deterministic routing rules that automatically assign the right queue and Parallel Investigations (PIs), then keep monitoring until auto‑closure.

The punchline is real impact: this system has helped resolve ~29,000 incidents in last 6 months through automation-driven handling. We’ll translate that into what it means operationally—fewer repetitive triage loops, faster time-to-action, and more engineer time returned to higher-value work.

Beyond the “what,” the talk focuses on the “how to drive change”: picking the highest-leverage pain point, designing safe automation with guardrails (rule priority, exclusions, history-based PI discovery), and closing the loop with monitoring so the system doesn’t just route— it finishes the job.
